T-Systems OTC.summary_note:
T-Systems Open Telekom Cloud (OTC) is Deutsche Telekom's original public cloud platform, launched in 2016 in direct partnership with Huawei Technologies using Huawei FusionSphere as the core cloud operating system. Its sovereignty profile reflects this heritage: strong in legal jurisdiction and EU corporate governance, but materially compromised at the infrastructure and technology layers by a structural and unresolved dependency on Huawei, a Chinese company subject to China's National Intelligence Law (2017). OTC earns genuine high marks for German/EU legal governance (no US CLOUD Act exposure), EU data residency (Biere and Magdeburg data centres exclusively), a comprehensive certification stack (BSI C5 Type 2, ISO 27001/27018/27701, SOC 1/2/3 Type II, TISAX, EU COC), OpenStack-based workload portability, renewable energy (100% green power, PUE ~1.3), and GAIA-X founding membership. Customer-managed encryption via KMS (BYOK) is also a genuine strength.

However, OTC's critical sovereignty deficits originate from the Huawei FusionSphere dependency. The core cloud OS, server hardware, firmware, and third-level support all involve Huawei — a Chinese-controlled vendor whose obligations under China's National Intelligence Law cannot be contractually overridden by T-Systems. The proprietary FusionSphere layer cannot be independently audited at source-code level even by T-Systems, and without Huawei software support OTC cannot be maintained as a platform. There is no dual-vendor OS strategy for OTC and no active remediation programme: Deutsche Telekom's response to this problem is T Cloud Public, a separately built platform, not an OTC upgrade. Key distinctions from T Cloud Public: SOV-1 Q1 receives P (not Y) because Huawei has decisive technical authority over the platform OS; SOV-4 Q2 receives N (not P) because OTC cannot be maintained without Huawei third-level involvement, with no EU alternative planned; SOV-5 Q3 receives P (not N) because T-Systems EU staff review and apply all updates from EU, even though the FusionSphere OS is packaged by Huawei; SOV-7 Q5 receives P because FusionSphere patches originate from Huawei, introducing a non-EU element into patch management.

OTC and T Cloud Public share the same physical data centres (Biere, Magdeburg), environmental practices, and Deutsche Telekom SOC infrastructure, which explains why their SOV-3 (data residency), SOV-7 (security certifications), and SOV-8 (environmental) verdicts are comparable despite architectural divergence. Deutsche Telekom's explicit strategy is to migrate OTC customers to T Cloud Public and allow OTC to diminish in strategic importance — OTC's sovereignty profile is therefore frozen at its current state while T Cloud Public's is actively improving.
